title: Farnesoid X receptor activation protects against renal fibrosis via modulation of β-catenin signaling

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states "Treatment with the FXR agonist CDCA or GW4064 decreased body weight, renal lipid accumulation, as well as renal injury" in HFD-fed mice, and "renal β-catenin signaling was activated and improved with FXR-agonist treatment in HFD-fed mice." However, the Methods describe only four in vivo groups: control diet, HFD, HFD + 0.1% CDCA, and HFD + 30 mg/kg INT-747 (OCA). GW4064 was used only in vitro, so the in vivo claim about GW4064 is unsupported/contradicted by the described design.

The abstract states mice "were fed by a 60% kcal fat diet for 20 weeks", whereas the Methods state mice were purchased at 5 weeks, randomized after 3 weeks (i.e., at 8 weeks of age), and killed "after a 12-week treatment" with urine collected at week 20 (of age). The actual HFD exposure described is 12 weeks, not 20 weeks.

The text writes "lysyl oxidase (LOX)-1-related oxidative stress". LOX-1 is the lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 (OLR1), an entirely different protein from lysyl oxidase (LOX). The cited mechanism of ox-LDL-induced injury is misattributed to the wrong enzyme/receptor.

The paper states OCA (INT-747) "was developed for the treatment of various liver diseases, including biliary atresia and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis". OCA is approved/developed for primary biliary cholangitis (and investigated in NASH), not biliary atresia; this is a factual misstatement of the drug's indication attributed to the cited references.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, Figure 2 description vs. Figure 3 description
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In the Figure 2 results the authors report "a 1.3-fold induction of fibronectin protein stimulated by ox-LDL", whereas in the Figure 3 results they report that ICG-001 "attenuated 1.6-fold fibronectin production by ox-LDL". The same ox-LDL-induced fibronectin induction is quantified with two different, unexplained values.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 3B (quantification) vs. Results text on ICG-001
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 3B shows fibronectin values of DMSO = 1.0, DMSO+ox-LDL = 2.0, ICG-001+ox-LDL = 1.25, i.e., a 2.0-fold ox-LDL induction, while the text states ox-LDL induced 1.6-fold fibronectin production.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 3G vs. Results text on TOPflash activity
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states "exogenous FXR inhibited the 1.7-fold transcriptional activity induced by ox-LDL", but Figure 3G shows pcDNA3 = 1.0 and pcDNA3+ox-LDL = 2.0 (a 2.0-fold induction), contradicting the stated fold-change.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 3J vs. Results text on FXR siRNA
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Text: "FXR siRNA could increase 1.3-fold β-catenin transcriptional activity"; Figure 3J shows control siRNA = 1.0 and FXR siRNA = 1.4. The quantified values disagree.

The results refer to "Expression of FXR, pDEL-FXR and pβ-catenin ... confirmed by Western blotting with anti-flag", but no deletion construct (pDEL-FXR, presumably an AF1-domain deletion) is described anywhere in the Methods (only pcDNA3, pcDNA3-flag-FXR and pCMV3-C-flag-β-catenin are listed). The key domain-mapping reagent underpinning the AF1 conclusion is undescribed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (last Results sentence) and Results, Figure 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract concludes "FXR could bind with β-catenin via the AF1 domain, and disrupt the assembly of the core β-catenin/TCF4 complex", yet the reported experiments only show FXR/β-catenin co-localization, co-immunoprecipitation and TOPflash reporter effects. No TCF4 binding/complex-disruption assay or domain-mapping experiment is described in the Methods or Results, so this conclusion is not supported by the presented evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, paragraph following Figure 3 ("FXR is a key factor for the stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This conclusion contradicts the authors' own data statement two paragraphs earlier: "The alteration of FXR activation did not affect cellular β-catenin levels". If total β-catenin levels are unchanged, FXR cannot be claimed to be a key factor for β-catenin stabilization.

The Methods state each group had n = 6 and that one HFD mouse was found dead at 15 weeks of age, yet no adjustment of group size (HFD n = 5) is reported anywhere, and all analyses are presented as if the original group sizes applied. The actual analyzed n for the HFD group is never stated.

Figure 1C is described as showing that nuclear FXR staining is decreased after 6 h of ox-LDL stimulation, whereas Figure 4A is described as showing FXR and β-catenin co-localized in the nucleus of ox-LDL-stimulated cells. The two immunofluorescence results about nuclear FXR after ox-LDL are presented without reconciliation and appear contradictory.
